rows.text: Turning Multipath into Positioning Information:
Persistent Electromagnetic-Twin DoA Localization
Tuo Wu, Zhentian Zhang, Ye Tian, and Hing Cheung So, Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—Reflected paths can support localization when line-
of-sight (LoS) links are blocked, but their usefulness depends on
how accurately the stored model predicts their directions. This
paper develops electromagnetic-twin (ET) direction-of-arrival
(DoA) localization with a persistent, physically calibrated path-
angle field. A nominal floor plan supplies virtual-path geometry,
and sparse reference probes at known positions learn a com-
pact directional correction. Field order and regularization are
selected from calibration data alone. For each user, unordered
DoAs are processed by joint position estimation and one-to-one
path association, using assignment-aware multistart search and
robust Gauss–Newton refinement. New trusted probes update
the stored correction through recursive least squares (RLS),
without reprocessing all previous measurements. The analysis
establishes calibration rank conditions, objective descent, and
conditional information gains from reflected paths, while also dis-
tinguishing the decay of initialization bias from the convergence
of localization error. Synthetic experiments use 500 queries per
operating point. At 50% LoS blockage and 1.5◦ DoA error, the
calibrated ET achieves 0.39 m root-mean-square error, versus
0.55 m for nominal geometry. After a wall change, its final error
is 0.43 m, versus 0.63 m for a frozen calibrated map. Equal-
evidence comparisons show competitive calibrated alternatives
and faster abrupt-change recovery with sliding-window updates
than with the configured RLS. The results support reusable
directional calibration, not a universally superior map or update
rule, and validation is limited to synthetic first-order reflections
with trusted calibration labels.
Index Terms—Electromagnetic twin, direction-of-arrival,
multipath-assisted localization, virtual anchor, path association,
robust positioning, Fisher information, online calibration.
I. INTRODUCTION

Combined angle and delay measurements can further support

and three-dimensional indoor positioning [3], [4]. The accu-
racy of these estimates depends not only on measurement noise

but also on the available propagation geometry, as established
by information analysis of localization accuracy [5]. In indoor
environments, however, walls and obstacles may block direct
links while producing several reflected arrivals. How to use
these arrivals reliably is therefore an important question for
maintaining positioning service.
Multipath can be treated as either an impairment or a source
of geometric information. Rejecting non-line-of-sight (NLoS)
measurements protects an estimator designed for direct prop-
agation, but may leave too few independent bearings when
line-of-sight (LoS) links are blocked. Alternatively, a specular
reflection can be represented through a mirrored anchor or
user, allowing the reflected direction to constrain position.
Leitinger et al. [6] quantified the position-related information
in multipath components, while Meissner et al. [7] evaluated
multipath-assisted indoor navigation using measured ultra-
wideband signals. These results support using suitable re-
flected paths rather than discarding all NLoS observations [8].
For angle-based localization, multipath-aware reference mod-
els likewise provide information beyond direct bearings [9].
When reflector locations are unknown, simultaneous local-
ization and mapping (SLAM) can estimate the user and envi-
ronmental features together. Channel-SLAM [10] and belief-
propagation-based multipath SLAM [11] exploit the consis-
tency of propagation paths across observations. Related work
extends this principle to situational awareness in millimeter-
wave massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) sys-
tems [12]. These studies establish that propagation structure
can be learned and reused. A complementary situation arises
when an initial floor plan is already available but does not
accurately predict the measured directions. In that case, dis-
covering the entire environment again may be unnecessary,
while the immediate task is to calibrate the useful paths in the
existing model.
Environment-dependent radio knowledge can also be re-
tained without explicitly estimating reflector geometry. Chan-
nel charting constructs a radio representation from accumu-
lated channel state information (CSI) [13], and channel
knowledge maps (CKMs) organize location-indexed channel
descriptors for subsequent communication tasks [14]. Digital-
twin-assisted fingerprinting further uses a digital replica to
generate location-dependent MIMO signatures [15]. These
approaches offer different interfaces for reusing environmental
information. Their accuracy in a physical site nevertheless
depends on the agreement between the retained representation
and the observations available during operation.
